name: Lebanon
summary_text: Lebanon is dangerous for trans visitors — the Arab world's most socially open country layered over one of its most explicitly anti-trans statutes. Article 521 of the Penal Code prescribes up to six years' imprisonment for “men disguising themselves as women” — a direct criminalisation of trans feminine expression. Article 534 (“intercourse contrary to the order of nature,” up to 1 year) remains in force though several courts have ruled it inapplicable to same-sex relations. Courts have granted legal gender recognition in some post-surgery cases since 1987, but inconsistently. Beirut's queer scene is the region's most visible — bars, NGOs (Helem, Proud Lebanon), and a documented court history — but the climate deteriorated sharply since 2022: state-affiliated militia groups attacked queer venues after an anti-discrimination bill was introduced, and Cairo 52 documents rising prejudice and violence against trans people, particularly trans women, who face entrenched marginalisation and family/community violence. For a visitor: Beirut is navigable with discretion; visible trans feminine expression carries real (statutory) arrest risk; the economic collapse has degraded police predictability in both directions.

sources.title: Lebanon | Cairo 52 Legal Research Institute
sources.claim_summary: Cairo 52 country review of Lebanon: de facto and explicit criminalisation of trans expression (especially trans women) under Penal Code provisions; rising prejudice and violence in Beirut including attacks by state-affiliated militia groups on queer spaces after a decriminalisation bill was introduced; gradual progress on legal gender recognition since a 2015 judge's ruling emphasising the significance of transitioning; gender-affirming healthcare not prohibited and comparatively accessible, though privatised healthcare limits options.

sources.title: 7.5. LGBTIQ persons, including activists | European Union Agency for Asylum
sources.claim_summary: EUAA Lebanon Country Focus, section 7.5 'LGBTIQ persons, including activists': assessment of the situation of LGBTIQ persons in Lebanon.

sources.title: Tough Territory for Transgender People in the Middle East and North Africa | Human Rights Watch
sources.claim_summary: Human Rights Watch (Apr 2022): 'Tough Territory for Transgender People in the Middle East and North Africa' — regional survey incl. Lebanon on LGR requirements and enforcement.

sources.title: Confused Judiciary & Transgender Rights: Inside the MENA Region’s Case Law on Legal Gender Recognition • Manara Magazine
sources.claim_summary: Manara Magazine essay by Nora Noralla (March 2022): 'Confused Judiciary & Transgender Rights' - inside MENA case law on legal gender recognition in Lebanon, Egypt, Kuwait and the UAE; no legislative framework forces trans people into lengthy, costly judicial review where judges rely on outdated medical practices, selective Sharia readings and socio-religious bias, producing inconsistent rulings.

sources.title: Lebanon | Outright International
sources.claim_summary: Outright International country overview (updated March 2026): Article 534 ('sexual intercourse contrary to the order of nature') is regularly used for arrests; several courts have ruled it does not apply to same-sex relations but it remains in force; trans people can change markers only after surgical procedures; in June 2022 the Interior Ministry banned gatherings 'promoting sexual perversion'; the 'soldiers of God' group attacked queer bars and drag shows; Helem denounced the 2024 murder of a trans woman.

sources.title: Lebanon: Police Shutter Pride Events | Human Rights Watch
sources.claim_summary: HRW (May 2018): 'Lebanon: Police Shutter Pride Events' - security forces forced cancellation of Beirut Pride events and detained organisers, using 'debauchery' charges and pressure on venues.

sources.title: Inside Georges Azzi’s Brave Fight for LGBT Rights in the Middle East
sources.claim_summary: The Daily Beast (May 2018): profile of Georges Azzi - co-founder of Helem (the first LGBT advocacy group in the Arab world, 2004), repeatedly dragged to Beirut police stations for interrogation and psychological pressure; now executive director of the Arab Foundation for Freedoms and Equality, campaigning across MENA; received OutRight's Felipa De Souza Award.

sources.title: Lebanon Edges Closer to Decriminalizing Same-sex Conduct | Human Rights Watch
sources.claim_summary: HRW (Feb 2017): 'Lebanon Edges Closer to Decriminalizing Same-Sex Conduct' - a judge ruled that consensual same-sex conduct is not 'against nature', building on earlier rulings interpreting Article 534 narrowly.
